analysis.one_liner: Bans interest charges on debt paid on time and caps credit card rate hikes and fees.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on May 15, 2007, received no further action, and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for credit cards. It banned charging interest on debt a cardholder pays on time, limited how much a card company could raise a rate as a penalty (no more than 7 points above the old rate), and made any rate increase apply only to new borrowing, not to the balance already owed. It also forced payments to go first to the highest-interest balance, restricted over-the-limit fees, barred fees just for paying a bill, and required annual audits of card companies' billing practices. The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Cardholders who carry balances or occasionally pay late. The bill would have stopped card companies from charging interest on debt already paid off, limited surprise penalty rate increases to 7 percentage points, and stopped raising rates on balances built up before the increase. It also would have cut down on stacked fees, since payments would have to be applied to the highest-interest debt first and over-limit fees could only be charged once per cycle in most cases.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits charging interest on debt that a cardholder repays within the grace period, ending double-cycle billing on amounts already paid [S2][S3].
Caps penalty rate increases at 7 percentage points above the rate in effect before the penalty, and makes rate increases apply only to new borrowing, not to existing balances [S2][S3].
Requires payments to be applied first to the balance with the highest interest rate, rather than to the cheapest debt first, which reduces total interest for cardholders with mixed balances [S2][S3].
Restricts over-the-limit fees, bars fees charged just for paying a bill by mail, phone, or online, and requires currency-exchange fees to reflect actual cost [S2][S3].

Requires each card issuer's federal regulator to audit the issuer's credit card operations annually, reviewing samples of billing statements and payment applications, and to require corrective action [S2][S3].

Directs the Federal Reserve to report annually to Congress on the profitability of card issuers, including how much income comes from high-rate interest (25 percent or more) and from fees on cardholders and merchants [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and other lenders that profit from interest charged on paid-off balances, penalty rate increases on existing balances, interest on fees, multiple over-limit charges, and pay-to-pay fees. Merchants also pay card-interchange fees indirectly, though the bill does not directly cap those; the new Fed profitability report would have itemized income from merchant fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuing banks and lenders

drawbacks.text: Restricting interest and fee collection reduces issuer revenue, and some issuers respond by tightening who can get cards or raising base rates — the bill's limits on rate increases could push lenders to price in more risk up front [S3].

The bill adds compliance and audit work: annual regulator audits with statement sampling and detailed new data reporting to the Federal Reserve impose administrative costs on issuers and regulators [S2][S3].

A cardholder's own good-faith objection: letting cardholders choose a fixed limit that cannot be exceeded is genuinely protective, but it may make it harder for some users to complete legitimate transactions near their limit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to cardholders are direct and concrete: the bill targeted practices — charging interest on debt already repaid, ratcheting up rates on old balances, stacking fees — that cost ordinary households real money. The costs fall on the credit card industry and show up as higher advertised rates or tighter approval for some borrowers. The bill is straightforwardly designed; its main weakness is that it predates later, broader reforms and relies on regulator audits that could be unevenly enforced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Carl Levin introduced the bill on May 15, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
The bill's only actions were introduction and referral; the committee never took it up and no vote was ever scheduled [S5].
It had 10 cosponsors (9 Democrats and 1 Independent) but died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept the practices the bill targeted — charging interest on paid-off balances, raising rates on old debt, and stacking fees — for the rest of the Congress. Cardholders continued paying them. Related provisions eventually became law separately in 2009, but this bill itself never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers kept their fee practices

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 10 cosponsors — 9 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no Republican cosponsors listed; with no votes or committee action recorded, the partisan shape is unclear beyond the sponsor's party [S4].

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and consumer lenders)
industries.note: The bill would have cut several major revenue streams: interest on balances already repaid, penalty rate hikes on existing debt, interest charged on fees, multiple over-limit charges, and pay-to-pay fees. It also would have made their pricing more transparent through required audits and annual Fed profitability reports [S2][S3].

Merchants pay card-interchange fees that issuers fund partly through cardholder revenue; the bill did not cap those fees directly, but its annual Fed report would have itemized issuer income from merchant fees, increasing scrutiny. Consumers paying less to issuers would have more to spend [S3].
